classification.difficultyReason: Translate linked verbal relationships into three-set regions, distinguish a total intersection from its exclusive region, and solve for the triple overlap before finding French only.

content.prompt: In a school of 650 everybody studies French ($F$), German ($G$) or Indonesian ($I$). All but 41 study French, 12 study French and Indonesian but not German. Thirteen study Indonesian and German but not French and the same number study German only. Twice as many study French and German but not Indonesian as study all three. The number studying Indonesian only is the same as the total studying both French and German. What is the probability that a student chosen at random studies French only?

answer.short:
$\frac{291}{325}$

There are 582 students who study French only, out of 650 students.
answer.worked:
Let $x$ be the number studying all three languages. Then $2x$ study French and German but not Indonesian, so $3x$ study both French and German in total. Thus $3x$ also study Indonesian only.

The 41 students who do not study French consist of Indonesian only, German only, and Indonesian and German but not French:

$$\begin{align*}3x+13+13&=41\\3x+26&=41\\3x&=15\\x&=5.\end{align*}$$

There are $650-41=609$ students studying French. Of these, 12 study French and Indonesian only, 10 study French and German only, and 5 study all three.

$$\begin{align*}n(\text{French only})&=609-12-10-5\\n(\text{French only})&=582\\P(\text{French only})&=\frac{582}{650}\\P(\text{French only})&=\frac{291}{325}.\end{align*}$$
